paper.title: C 3 : Rethinking Process Supervision via Confidence-Guided Credit Correction in Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Large language models are increasingly trained as multi-turn agents that interact with external tools. However, outcome-only reinforcement learning can produce a form of misguided reinforcement : even on successful trajectories, undesirable local behaviors may receive positive token-level advantages and be favored by the policy update.
To address this issue, we propose Confidence-Guided Credit Correction (C 3 ) , a plug-in method for local credit correction. C 3 identifies spans corresponding to undesirable behaviors and selectively corrects positive credit after advantage estimation, with the correction strength adaptively controlled by the behavior policy’s confidence in the corresponding behavior, while leaving the task reward and original credit estimation unchanged.
Across multiple multi-turn benchmarks, C 3 improves performance under both critic-based and critic-free reinforcement learning methods. Injecting the same behavioral signals as turn-level or outcome rewards does not consistently improve performance. Our results show that local credit correction provides an effective form of process supervision for outcome-driven RL.

However, outcome-only reinforcement learning can produce a form of misguided reinforcement : even on successful trajectories, undesirable local behaviors may receive positive token-level advantages and be favored by the policy update. To address this issue, we propose Confidence-Guided Credit Correction (C 3 ) , a plug-in method for local credit correction. C 3 identifies spans corresponding to undesirable behaviors and selectively corrects positive credit after advantage estimation, with the correction strength adaptively controlled by the behavior policy’s confidence in the corresponding behavior, while leaving the task reward and original credit estimation unchanged. Across multiple multi-turn benchmarks, C 3 improves performance under both critic-based and critic-free reinforcement learning methods. Injecting the same behavioral signals as turn-level or outcome rewards does not consistently improve performance. Our results show that local credit correction provides an effective form of process supervision for outcome-driven RL. 1 Introduction Multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for training language agents on complex tasks that require long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool interaction ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Jian et al., 2026 ) . A common approach optimizes agents with outcome-level rewards that evaluate the success of an entire interaction trajectory ( Jin et al., 2025 ) . However, outcome-level supervision provides only sparse and coarse-grained feedback for intermediate behaviors, making it difficult to assign appropriate credit across long-horizon interactions ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . To provide denser supervision for intermediate behaviors, recent work introduces process-level rewards and other process-level signals ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . (a) Mixed credit in undesirable behaviors. (b) Credit construction across optimization paradigms. Figure 1: Misguided reinforcement under outcome-only training. (a) Incorrect tool use and redundant search receive mixed token-level credit, with positive and negative advantages shown in rose and blue-grey . (b) Token-level credit construction in critic-based and critic-free optimization. Our Key Observation. We inspect representative training trajectories under outcome-only training and find that undesirable local behaviors can still receive positive token-level advantages. We identify this phenomenon as a form of misguided reinforcement . More precisely, it is a form of local credit misalignment, where the token-level advantage assigned to an undesirable behavior is inconsistent with its process-level quality. This creates a fundamental mismatch between what behavior should be discouraged and what the policy update favors . Figure 1 (a) shows two representative undesirable behaviors observed. In the invalid tool call, a missing closing tag for <search> causes the call to be malformed, yet the preceding unclosed tokens receive positive advantages while the subsequently closed tokens receive negative advantages. In the redundant search, the same query is issued in consecutive turns, but its tokens also receive mixed advantages. Such misalignment reflects the challenge of assigning localized credit from trajectory-level outcomes. Why Existing Credit Construction Falls Short. Figure 1 (b) illustrates how token-level credit is constructed under two common optimization paradigms. In critic-based reinforcement learning, token-level advantages are estimated through returns and value functions, so a process-level penalty can propagate to tokens beyond the behavior that triggered it. In critic-free methods, relative advantages are derived directly from trajectory-level outcomes, causing local behaviors to inherit credit from the overall trajectory. Thus, the two paradigms differ in how credit is constructed, but share a more fundamental challenge: How can process-level supervision correct a localized undesirable behavior without altering the credit assigned to unrelated behaviors, thereby avoiding credit misalignment? To address this challenge, we propose C 3 (Confidence-Guided Credit Correction) , a lightweight process-level credit correction module that directly operates on token-level advantages. Given undesirable behaviors localized by external process-level supervision, C 3 selectively corrects positive advantages within the corresponding spans, with the correction magnitude adapting to the model’s confidence in the corresponding actions. C 3 introduces no additional process rewards and does not modify the underlying policy optimization objective, making it a plug-in module applicable to both critic-based and critic-free reinforcement learning paradigms. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify and characterize misguided reinforcement, where undesirable local behaviors can receive positive policy advantages under outcome-level training, creating a mismatch between behavioral quality and the direction of policy updates. • We propose C 3 , a plug-and-play confidence-guided credit correction framework that rectifies misaligned positive credit within detector-localized undesirable behavior spans without altering task rewards or the underlying RL objective. • We evaluate C 3 across different policy optimization paradigms and multi-turn agent benchmarks. Results show that C 3 reduces positive advantages on detected undesirable-behavior spans, decreases their occurrence, and improves overall agent performance. 2 Related Work Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents. Language agents are commonly optimized with critic-based methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) or group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . They support retrieval ( Jin et al., 2025 ) and long-horizon research or collaboration ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) , but typically learn from trajectory-level outcomes. Consequently, an otherwise successful trajectory may still reinforce undesirable intermediate behaviors. Unlike approaches that modify the overall policy optimization process, C 3 preserves the underlying objective and instead performs localized credit correction on undesirable behavior spans. Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn Agents. Credit assignment asks how trajectory-level outcome credit should be attributed to intermediate actions. Hierarchical methods allocate credit across turns ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) , while turn- or step-level estimators align advantages with action boundaries ( Li et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Action-to-token allocation further refines the mapping from outcomes to local advantages ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and retrospective methods estimate each turn’s contribution ( Ekbote et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) . C 3 leaves this outcome-to-advantage mapping intact and operates on the resulting token-level advantages. While these approaches refine how outcome credit is distributed, C 3 instead focuses on whether the resulting local credit is consistent with the underlying behavior. Process Supervision for LLM Agents. Process supervision instead asks whether an intermediate behavior is desirable. Process reward models score individual steps ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) ; search agents use step-wise rewards ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , information gain ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , or hindsight signals ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . Judges and self-distillation provide local assessments ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026 ) , while counterfactual attribution derives feedback from alternative rollouts ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . These signals are typically introduced as rewards or advantage shaping. Rather than introducing additional process rewards, C 3 uses localized process feedback to correct positive advantages assigned to undesirable-behavior spans within the existing token-level advantage. 3 Preliminary We consider a multi-turn reinforcement learning setting where an LLM agent interacts with an environment to solve a task. Generally, most positive-advantage tokens correspond to behaviors that are consistent with successful task completion. However, a small subset of tokens may exhibit undesirable behaviors yet receive positive advantages, causing them to be reinforced by the base RL objective. C 3 targets these sparse misassignments by selectively calibrating their advantages, while leaving the remaining tokens, the reward function, and the base advantage estimator unchanged. 4 Methodology We define C 3 as a post-estimation operator for multi-turn agent reinforcement learning. An external transcript detector localizes an undesirable behavior , the base RL pipeline provides token-level advantages, and C 3 corrects these advantages before the actor update. We first motivate this design through an empirical behavioral and credit audit, and then define the inputs, localization rule, and correction operator. Figure 2 summarizes the resulting workflow. A detector localizes an undesirable-behavior span, the actor-side correction is applied only within that span, and its strength follows the policy confidence. 4.1 Motivation: Misguided Reinforcement and Local Credit We investigate local credit dynamics through two representative undesirable behaviors, invalid actions and query loops , whose operational definitions and detection rules are provided in Appendix B.1 . Figure 1 (a) illustrates representative event-level examples, while Figure 3 traces how undesirable-behavior occurrence and token-level advantages evolve during RL training. (a) PPO training (b) GDPO training (c) Positive-credit audit Figure 3: Misguided reinforcement during RL training. Observation 1: Undesirable behaviors reveal complex credit dynamics. As shown in Figure 3 (a,b), undesirable-behavior occurrence generally decreases during training for critic-based PPO, whereas critic-free GDPO shows no consistent decline and even rebounds at the later stage. PPO derives token-level advantages through a learned critic and GAE, while GDPO constructs relative advantages from group-level trajectory signals that combine task outcomes with undesirable-behavior penalties. These contrasting dynamics suggest that the same undesirable behaviors can evolve differently under different credit construction mechanisms, making local credit assignment inherently nontrivial. Observation 2: Behavior suppression does not imply local credit alignment. Figure 3 (c) shows that, among 63,511 63{,}511 valid tokens within detector-identified undesirable-behavior spans in an instrumented PPO run, 18,460 18{,}460 receive positive base advantage before correction, corresponding to 29.07%. Notably, this positive credit persists even as the number of undesirable-behavior tokens decreases during training. This indicates that reducing undesirable-behavior occurrence does not eliminate incorrect local credit, suggesting that trajectory-level supervision can still assign positive local credit to undesirable behaviors. Together, these observations expose a failure mode in multi-turn RL: undesirable behaviors can remain positively reinforced at the token level even as they are suppressed at the trajectory level. The contrasting dynamics under PPO and GDPO further suggest that this issue is not specific to a particular credit construction mechanism, but can arise whenever trajectory-level signals are translated into local credit. This motivates a targeted intervention: Instead of redesigning rewards or advantage estimation, can correcting positive credit for a small number of localized undesirable behaviors be sufficient to improve RL? 4.2 Local Credit Correction Motivated by the local credit misalignment identified above, we aim to correct policy credit only where its direction is inconsistent with the detected local behavior, while preserving the credit assigned to the remaining parts of the trajectory. For multi-turn search question answering, we use Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) with the SLIME framework ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . The agent interacts with a retrieval environment built on the Wiki-Fixed corpus introduced in ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , using Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) with 4096-dimensional embeddings and FAISS for retrieval. For WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , we use Qwen3-4B with full-parameter updates in the standard WebShop environment. All models are trained under their corresponding task protocols. Baselines. We evaluate C 3 under two optimization families: critic-based optimization and critic-free group-relative optimization . For critic-based optimization, we compare standard PPO, PPO with a turn-level process reward, and PPO with C 3 . The process-reward baseline incorporates detector events into return and advantage estimation, whereas C 3 directly corrects token-level advantages on detected spans. For critic-free group-relative optimization, we compare GDPO ( Liu et al., 2026 ) with and without C 3 . GDPO follows the group-relative paradigm of GRPO but decouples the normalization of individual reward components. Configurations are provided in Appendix B.2 . Evaluation Benchmarks and Metrics. For search question answering, we evaluate on seven multi-turn benchmarks: NQ ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) , TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) , PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) , HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2022 ) , and Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) . We report strict exact match (EM), with the overall score computed as the unweighted mean across the seven benchmarks. For WebShop, we report the task score and success rate on the fixed 500-instance benchmark split. 5.2 Main Results We evaluate C 3 on two multi-turn agent environments, Search QA and WebShop, under both critic-based PPO and critic-free GDPO, reporting both final task performance and training dynamics. Taken together, these results show that C 3 improves performance under both critic-based and critic-free optimization across the two multi-turn agent environments. The gains are reflected not only in final benchmark performance, but also in the training dynamics, where C 3 maintains stronger performance for longer before the late-stage degradation observed in the corresponding baselines . 6 Analysis We further analyze how C 3 changes agent behavior and evaluate its key design choices through undesirable-behavior analysis and confidence aggregation ablations. Additional experiments and case studies are provided in Appendices C and D . 6.1 Does C 3 Change Agent Behavior? We examine SFT, PPO, PPO with process reward, and PPO+C 3 on the same 51,713 51{,}713 Search QA questions under greedy decoding. Figure 6 separates invalid actions from query loops to examine how different types of undesirable behaviors respond to outcome-level training. (a) Undesirable-behavior rate (b) Query-loop share (c) Rate vs. accuracy Figure 6: Greedy evaluation on 51,713 51{,}713 questions per arm. PPO substantially reduces invalid actions relative to SFT, suggesting that straightforward tool-call failures can be effectively suppressed by trajectory-level training. Query loops, however, show a different pattern: the process-reward variant reaches a query-loop rate of 0.474 % 0.474\% , nearly 3 × 3\times that of PPO ( 0.159 % 0.159\% ), and 245 of its 247 flagged trajectories contain query loops. In contrast, PPO+C 3 reduces the query-loop rate to 0.064 % 0.064\% , a 2.5 × 2.5\times reduction relative to PPO and a 7.4 × 7.4\times reduction relative to the process-reward variant. These results suggest that trajectory-level training is effective for explicit action failures but less effective for redundant cross-turn behavior . C 3 complements this by correcting positive local credit on detected behavior spans, providing a more direct signal for behaviors that are not reliably suppressed by trajectory-level supervision. 6.2 Ablation of C 3 Design Choices C 3 uses policy confidence to determine the strength of local credit correction. C 3 addresses this through confidence-guided local credit correction, reversing positive advantages on detected undesirable-behavior spans while leaving the task reward, returns, and critic targets unchanged. Across experiments, C 3 improves average exact match and reduces detected undesirable behaviors, highlighting that effective process supervision is not only about providing denser behavioral feedback, but also about translating that feedback into appropriate local policy credit. Rather, after correcting credit on detected undesirable behaviors, the resulting policy can allocate retrieval differently depending on the information requirements of the task. In particular, reducing unnecessary interactions on simpler tasks does not preclude retaining additional retrieval on tasks that require multi-hop information gathering. The behavior under GDPO is different. Compared with outcome-only GDPO, GDPO+C 3 generally increases the number of searches across the benchmarks. This difference from PPO highlights that the behavioral effect of the same local credit correction is not invariant to the underlying optimization paradigm. PPO and GDPO construct token-level credit differently, so correcting the same type of local positive credit can lead to different changes in the resulting interaction policy. Importantly, the increase in search frequency under GDPO should not be interpreted as C 3 directly encouraging more retrieval, since retrieval frequency is not an explicit optimization target of the method. Taken together, these results show that C 3 does not impose a fixed preference for shorter or longer interaction trajectories . Instead, its behavioral effect emerges indirectly through local credit correction and varies with both the optimization paradigm and the task. This distinction is important because it suggests that the performance gains from C 3 should not be understood simply in terms of performing more or fewer tool interactions. C 3 changes which local behaviors receive policy credit, while the resulting interaction allocation is determined by the broader optimization process and task requirements.
